analysis.one_liner: Loosens FDA safety oversight of vitamins and herbal supplements and lets labels make disease-related health claims.
analysis.headline: Backed by 261 House cosponsors from both parties, the bill died in committee without a single vote before the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill defines vitamins, minerals, herbs, and amino acids as 'dietary supplements' and takes them out of the food-additive rules that otherwise require FDA safety approval before a new ingredient can be sold. It bars the FDA from setting maximum potency limits on supplements and lets labels describe a supplement's relationship to disease with 30 days' notice instead of pre-approval. It also requires fuller ingredient labels, sets 'Percent Daily Value' nutrition standards for food labels, and creates an Office of Dietary Supplements at the National Institutes of Health.
analysis.who_benefits: Vitamin, mineral, and herbal supplement makers gain the most: their ingredients escape the food-additive process that otherwise requires FDA safety review before sale, the FDA is barred from capping potency, and labels can characterize a supplement's relationship to disease after only 30 days' notice, with the agency forbidden from demanding supporting documentation beforehand [S2][S3]. Consumers who take supplements keep broad access to high-dose products and get more complete ingredient labels, and NIH gains a new research office funded at $5 million [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Defines dietary supplements as a distinct legal category covering vitamins, minerals, herbs, amino acids, and their extracts, and removes their ingredients from the definition of 'food additive,' which otherwise triggers pre-market safety approval.

Requires supplement labels to list each dietary ingredient and its quantity, identify the product as a supplement, and meet composition, quality, and purity standards, with violations treated as misbranding.
Requires food labels to declare 'Percent Daily Values' set to reflect intake that promotes optimal health, and no lower than the U.S. Recommended Daily Allowance.
Creates an Office of Dietary Supplements within the National Institutes of Health, authorized at $5 million for fiscal 1994, to coordinate research on supplements and disease prevention.

analysis.who_pays: The FDA gives up pre-market screening of supplement ingredients and its authority to cap potency or treat high-potency products as drugs; it can challenge unsafe products only after they are on the market, and must wait out a 60-day appeal period before suing, except where there is an imminent health hazard [S2][S3]. Consumers bear the risk that an ingredient or a health claim on the label turns out to be unsafe or unsupported, because safety documentation is submitted voluntarily and the burden falls on the government to prove danger after the fact.

drawbacks.text: Removing supplement ingredients from the food-additive rules means new ingredients can reach shelves without FDA reviewing safety evidence beforehand; the bill instead treats an ingredient as unsafe only if the Secretary has found, through rulemaking, a 'substantial and unreasonable risk' of illness or injury.

Labels may characterize a supplement's relationship to a disease with only 30 days' advance notice, and the bill says the Secretary 'may not impose any additional pre-market requirement' or ask for further documentation supporting the claim.

If the Secretary asserts a supplement violates the law, the United States cannot sue for 60 days while the manufacturer appeals, unless there is an imminent hazard to health, slowing enforcement against questionable products.

Supporters' best counterargument: the FDA in this period was moving to treat some supplement ingredients and health claims as unapproved drugs or food additives, which would have restricted consumer access to vitamins and herbs; the bill's defenders saw pre-approval requirements as a threat to products millions of people take daily. The honest cost an even-handed supporter must weigh is that the same loosening that protects access also lets unverified ingredients and disease-related claims reach consumers before anyone checks them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundles genuine consumer gains — full ingredient labeling, purity standards, better daily-value nutrition labels, and federal research on supplements — with a core trade that favors sellers: pre-market safety review is replaced by after-the-fact enforcement, potency caps are forbidden, and disease-related claims need only 30 days' notice. The labeling provisions are worth having; the safety structure shifts the burden of proof onto the government and, ultimately, onto consumers who discover problems only after taking a product. A better-designed version would have kept the labeling and research while preserving pre-market review of genuinely novel ingredients.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its health subcommittee — one hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and expired when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Richardson introduced the bill on April 7, 1993, with 14 original cosponsors from both parties, and was joined over the following months by members who added their names in waves through October 1993.
The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and, on May 12, 1993, to its Subcommittee on Health and the Environment.
The subcommittee held a hearing on July 29, 1993, but no markup or vote on the bill followed.
Richardson made further introductory remarks on the House floor in March and April 1994 while the bill continued to sit without action.

By the end of the 103rd Congress on January 3, 1995, 261 House members had cosponsored the bill — 125 Republicans and 135 Democrats — but it never received a committee vote or a floor vote, and bills that die at the end of a Congress carry over nowhere.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill mainly served supplement makers by stripping pre-market FDA review, its death left the FDA's existing authority over supplement ingredients and health claims unchanged for the time being. Consumers of supplements kept the status-quo oversight regime rather than the lighter one the bill would have created.

for.name: Rep. Bill Richardson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and promoted it with introductory remarks on the House floor in April 1993 and again in March and April 1994.

for.name: Vitamin and supplement industry
for.role: Manufacturers and trade groups of vitamins, minerals, and herbs
for.what_they_did: Backed congressional action to stop the FDA from treating supplement ingredients as unapproved drugs or food additives, mobilizing consumers in support; the bill's framework tracks that goal.

against.name: John Dingell
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired never reported the bill; it remained with the health subcommittee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Henry Waxman
against.role: Chair, Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, House Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: His subcommittee held one hearing on the bill in July 1993 but never scheduled a markup or vote on it.

against.name: Food and Drug Administration
against.role: Federal regulator of food and drug safety
against.what_they_did: Was then moving to treat some supplement ingredients and health claims as unapproved drugs or food additives; the bill was written to bar that approach, and the agency opposed the carve-out.

sides.party_line_note: The cosponsor list spanned both parties — 135 of 258 House Democrats and 125 of 176 House Republicans signed on — and no recorded vote on the bill ever occurred.

industries.industry: Dietary supplement manufacturers (vitamins, minerals, herbal products)
industries.note: The bill writes supplement makers a permanent protected category: their ingredients escape the food-additive process requiring pre-market FDA safety approval, the FDA is barred from capping potency, and labels can point to disease benefits with 30 days' notice instead of pre-approval. It does impose labeling and purity rules on them, but the core effect locks in a lighter-touch regime whose costs — unreviewed ingredients and unverified claims — fall on the consumers taking the products.

Supplements would be allowed to characterize their relationship to disease on labels without drug-level evidence, putting them in closer competition with medicines sold under far stricter testing requirements. Consumers choosing a supplement over a proven drug could lose access to effective treatment, though wider access to vitamins is what supporters intended.

The bill requires food labels to carry Percent Daily Values set at levels that promote optimal health, adding labeling costs for food companies while giving shoppers more complete nutrition information.
